title: Quasi-Phases of Quantum Matter
authors: Nick G. Jones, Paul Fendley, Nathanan Tantivasadakarn, Ruben Verresen
abstract: Within quantum many-body phase diagrams, continuous transition lines can appear and then terminate. However, it has remained unclear whether the neighboring regimes can be meaningfully described as distinct phases, akin to water and vapour, since any sharp characterization would have to go beyond the usual notion of phases of matter. We answer this in the affirmative by introducing quasi-phases: gapped regimes near a critical point that are connected in the broader phase diagram, but not by any gapped path accessible from small perturbations of the critical theory. The physical consequences include interface modes between regimes in the same phase of matter. More striking still, describing both the extended critical line and the gapped path connecting the regimes requires a bigger multicritical parent theory. In spin-chain examples with continuous terminating lines with central charge $c=1$, we find multicritical $c=3/2$ and $c=9/5$ orbifolds describing so-called 'quotient symmetry protected' and 'representation symmetry protected' topological phenomena. While one-dimensional symmetry-protected topological phases are labeled by projective representation classes, these quasi-phases can have interface modes carrying higher-dimensional linear representations. We turn this into a constructive principle through a weakening of the Lieb-Schultz-Mattis anomaly. Supporting distinct quasi-phases makes an unnecessary critical point infrared-necessary, even if it is unnecessary at the ultraviolet scale. This condition is more restrictive than simply having a codimension-one critical line, revealing richer structure within phases of matter than their conventional classification suggests.
summary: This paper introduces the concept of 'quasi-phases' to address ambiguities in classifying quantum matter near continuous critical points. It argues that distinct gapped regimes can exist even if they are connected by a critical line, provided the connection is not accessible via simple perturbations. This framework refines our understanding of phase diagrams by incorporating interface modes and stricter criteria for phase separation.
main_problem: To determine if neighboring gapped regimes separated by continuous critical lines constitute distinct physical phases, moving beyond conventional topological classifications.
main_result: The authors introduce 'quasi-phases,' defined by a specific path-connectedness criterion near a critical point, leading to a richer understanding of phase structure than previously thought.
method: The analysis involves studying the path-connectedness of gapped regimes via Renormalization Group (RG) flow arguments and developing a constructive principle by weakening the Lieb-Schultz-Mattis anomaly.
model_or_system: The study uses general quantum many-body systems, exemplified by 1+1D spin chains (like the XXZ chain) exhibiting Symmetry-Protected Topological (SPT) and Representation Symmetry Protected Topological (RSPT) phenomena.
key_observables: Interface modes, entanglement spectrum degeneracy, correlation length ($\xi$), and the necessity of certain critical points (IR-necessary criticality).
important_parameters: Staggering parameter ($\delta$), anisotropy ($\Delta$), and the central charge ($c$) of the critical theory.
main_assumptions: The core assumption is that the physical distinction between phases can be captured by the existence of a smooth interface connecting them in the RG flow neighborhood of the critical point.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the spectrum of the transfer matrix for spin chains and show interpolations of observables like correlation length across different Hamiltonian regimes.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the concept of quasi-phases, applies it to specific models like spin chains to analyze SPT/RSPT transitions, and culminates in establishing a general constructive principle for defining these richer phase structures.
why_interesting: The concept of quasi-phases provides a powerful, refined tool for classifying quantum matter that goes beyond simple topological invariants, directly impacting the understanding of phase transitions in strongly correlated systems.
